details:
**Song of myself**  
A free‑verse poem that opens Whitman’s seminal collection Leaves of Grass and famously declares, “I am large…I contain multitudes,” becoming an anthem of self‑celebration.

**Leaves of Grass**  
The evolving collection of Whitman’s poems, first published in 1855 and expanded in later editions, in which the poems “Song of myself,” “O Captain! My Captain!,” and “When Lilacs Last in the Dooryard Bloom’d” appear.

**Barbaric yawp**  
Whitman’s refrain, “I sound my barbaric yawp over the roofs of the world,” expressing his exuberant, expansive view of the American spirit.

**O Captain! My Captain!**  
A elegy written after Lincoln’s assassination, presented in the final “death‑bed” edition of Leaves of Grass and set in a ship’s deck.

**When Lilacs Last in the Dooryard Bloom’d**  
Whitman’s mourning poem for Abraham Lincoln, also in the final edition of Leaves of Grass.

**I am large, I contain multitudes**  
The opening line of “Song of myself,” capturing Whitman’s expansive sense of self and humanity.

**I Sing the Body Electric**  
A poem that celebrates the physical body, included in Leaves of Grass and reflecting Whitman’s belief in the unity of body and soul.

**Drum‑Taps**  
Whitman’s Civil‑War‑era anthology, largely written during his service as a volunteer nurse and featuring poems about the war’s violence and loss.

**Calamus poems**  
Whitman’s series of poems that explicitly celebrate same‑sex love, underscoring his openness about sexuality and his commitment to inclusivity.

**American poet**  
Whitman’s national identity, as he is frequently described as the “free‑verse poet” of the United States and the “poet of the nation.”

**I celebrate myself**  
The opening line of “Song of myself,” illustrating Whitman’s philosophy of self‑adulation and the celebration of individual experience.

**Out of the Cradle Endlessly Rocking**  
A poem in which a baby’s cradle rocks, representing the continuity of life, and often cited as an example of Whitman’s lyrical tenderness.
